claims.text: Plasma nitriding Ti-6Al-4V increases its surface hardness and wear resistance.
Plasma nitriding produces a uniform nanocrystalline layer rich in TiN and related titanium nitrides on Ti-6Al-4V.
The proposed treatment is nitrogen-plasma exposure at 600°C for 4 hours followed by controlled cooling.
The hardness and wear benefits should hold in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures.
The treatment forms a continuous surface layer primarily composed of TiN and sub-stoichiometric titanium nitrides.
Interstitial nitrogen diffuses into the near-surface region of Ti-6Al-4V.
Diffused nitrogen precipitates hard titanium-nitride phases.
The plasma-nitriding treatment refines the near-surface grain structure.
Solid-solution and precipitation strengthening increase resistance to plastic deformation and wear.
Surface hardness will increase by approximately 100–150% relative to untreated Ti-6Al-4V.
Plasma-nitrided Ti-6Al-4V will exhibit significantly lower wear depth than untreated Ti-6Al-4V.
The benefits depend on the nitride layer being uniform and sufficiently deep.
A nonuniform or excessively thin nitride layer may fail to improve hardness and wear resistance.
The quantitative improvement may vary with plasma-process parameters.
Long-term durability under cyclic or extreme conditions has not yet been validated.
The controlled experiment compares identically prepared plasma-nitrided and untreated Ti-6Al-4V sample sets.
Vickers microhardness profiles, wear depth, volume loss, and friction coefficient are the proposed response variables.
Failure to achieve at least about a 100% statistically significant hardness increase together with improved wear performance under both test conditions is intended to falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires a significant reduction in wear depth, but the falsification rule parenthetically describes 'corresponding improvement' as wear depths and friction coefficients comparable to those of the untreated alloy. Comparable performance is not an improvement and makes the wear criterion ambiguous.
